title: Evaluating Environmental DNA for Pacific Salmon Spawner Enumeration Across Diverse Freshwater Systems
content:
ABSTRACT

Advancing environmental DNA (eDNA) beyond species detection could provide scalable tools for estimating fish abundance, but the predictive relationships between eDNA concentration and abundance are often system-specific and influenced by highly variable environmental conditions. Here, we evaluated whether salmon (Oncorhynchus spp.) eDNA could predict spawner abundance across heterogeneous freshwater habitats by collecting eDNA samples, spawner counts and environmental measurements at 39 salmon spawning grounds and migratory routes across 28 stream and river systems in British Columbia, Canada. Salmon eDNA concentrations were strongly influenced by discharge and any relationship between eDNA and spawner counts was only evident after correcting eDNA concentrations for discharge. Discharge-corrected salmon eDNA positively but moderately predicted counts of live spawners (R 2 = 0.21), whereas dead salmon were not well predicted. We also show that in the absence of equipment-intensive discharge measurements, point measurements of flow velocity, particularly when measured at the centre of the channel, and channel width may be used as a sufficient discharge proxy. Water temperature and turbidity did not have clear effects on discharge-corrected salmon eDNA concentrations, but there was a positive association between salmon eDNA and bacterial eDNA. These results suggest that discharge-corrected eDNA concentrations can provide a useful but moderate index of live salmon spawner abundance across diverse lotic systems, while also demonstrating that further research into the relationships between eDNA and salmon abundance is needed before eDNA-based abundance estimates can be implemented within or replace conventional methods of stock assessment.
